subject: English Language
source: CISCE ICSE English Language (Paper 1) 2026 - Analysis of Pupil Performance (raw/LangPPA-26.pdf)

marking_schemes.question_text:
Write a composition (300 - 350 words) on the following:
Write an original short story beginning with the words: It was midnight and the doorbell rang...
marking_schemes.scheme_text: The story must be original and must begin with the words given. The story must have elements of mystery, suspense or humour and a surprise ending.
key_points: Begins with the exact given words: 'It was midnight and the doorbell rang...'
Elements of mystery, suspense or humour
common_errors: Did not begin with the given words, or rephrased/moved them mid-story
Wrote a first-person narrative essay instead of a story
Copied portions of the question or comprehension passage
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Many candidates did not begin the story with the given words; they rephrased the opening sentence or inserted it midway. Some struggled to maintain continuity in the narrative. Some wrote first-person narrative essays rather than stories, while others reproduced portions of the question or the comprehension passage instead of developing an original story.

writing_task.required_opening: It was midnight and the doorbell rang...
assessment_criteria: Relevance to the chosen topic and every part of the task addressed
Expression: vocabulary, sentence structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation

marking_schemes.question_text:
Write a composition (300 - 350 words) on the following:
If you could change one period in your school timetable, which one would you choose? Why do you think it needs to be changed and with which subject or activity would you replace it?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: This is a first person account and must be narrated from within the plausible experience of a Class X candidate. The change must be in a subject taught in school and may include co-curricular activities. Reasons for change must be clearly given and the replaced subject or activity should be clearly named.
key_points: First-person account within the plausible experience of a Class X candidate
Names the period/subject taught in school to be changed (may include co-curricular activities)
Clearly names the replacement subject or activity
common_errors: Did not name the replacement subject or activity
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Some candidates failed to clearly mention the subject they proposed to introduce in place of the existing one. Academically demanding subjects were often identified as 'burdensome'; Physical Education was a popular choice. Most grasped the essence and explained their reasons adequately even where linguistic proficiency was limited.

assessment_criteria: Relevance to the chosen topic and every part of the task addressed
Expression: vocabulary, sentence structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation

marking_schemes.question_text:
Write a composition (300 - 350 words) on the following:
You and your family enjoy eating out. Give a description of your favourite restaurant or food stall, and the sights and smells that attract you to the place. Explain why you like eating here.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Words of sight and smell must form the main body of this composition. There should be a description of the restaurant/food. Why that particular restaurant is special to the narrator must be explained.
key_points: Words of sight and smell form the main body
Description of the restaurant/food stall and its food
Explains why this particular place is special to the narrator
common_errors: Described the building/interiors instead of the food
Named several restaurants instead of focusing on one
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Many candidates devoted most of their essays to describing the building and interiors rather than the food; the sensory experience of the food (aroma, taste, texture) deserved more emphasis. Some named several restaurants instead of one; others described a single visit. Errors such as 'Me and my family', there/their confusion and misspelling 'restaurant' and 'necessary' were noted.

assessment_criteria: Relevance to the chosen topic and every part of the task addressed
Expression: vocabulary, sentence structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation

marking_schemes.question_text:
Write a composition (300 - 350 words) on the following:
'Homework is a necessary evil.'
Express your views either for or against this statement.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Views either for or against. The candidate should take a clear stand and give valid reasons for whatever stand he/she takes. A cohesive well-constructed logical argument and ideas based on logical reasoning and personal experience.
key_points: Takes one clear stand, either for or against
Cohesive, logical argument drawing on reasoning and personal experience
common_errors: No clear stand / argued both sides
Misunderstood 'necessary evil' and contradicted own stand
Too few examples to substantiate views
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Most took a clear stand, the majority against the motion, stressing the need for rest after a rigorous schedule. A few failed to take a clear stand or argued both sides; some gave inadequate examples. 'Necessary evil' was not understood by a few, who stated disagreement but then argued in support of the statement.

assessment_criteria: Relevance to the chosen topic and every part of the task addressed
Expression: vocabulary, sentence structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation

marking_schemes.question_text:
Write a composition (300 - 350 words) on the following:
Study the picture given below. Write a story or a description or an account of what it suggests to you. Your composition may be about the subject of the picture, or you may take suggestions from it; however, there must be a clear connection between the picture and your composition.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: Accept a wide interpretation. Any relevant ideas taken from the picture is to be accepted. However, a mere itemization / listing / description of the picture is to be penalized.
key_points: Clear connection between the picture and the composition
Wide interpretation accepted: story, description or account
Not a mere itemisation/listing/description of the picture
common_errors: Itemised or merely described the picture
No clear connection between picture and composition
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: The least attempted topic. Themes included childhood, poverty, the joy of simplicity, ingenuity, protection and sharing among siblings. Some resorted to itemisation rather than a coherent narrative; others merely described the picture without developing the ideas it suggested.

assessment_criteria: Relevance to the chosen topic and every part of the task addressed
Expression: vocabulary, sentence structure, grammar, spelling and punctuation
penalised: Mere itemisation / listing / description of the picture

marking_schemes.question_text: Your examinations are drawing near, and you would like to form a study group. Write a letter to one of your classmates inviting him or her to join it. Give details of how you plan to revise and explain why it would be helpful.
marking_schemes.scheme_text:
Format (Friendly/Informal letter)
Content
Invitation: e.g. please come / I invite you / we would like you to join (Any one)
Details of the study group / how you plan to revise: e.g. topic-wise discussion / shared notes / using online devices / discussion / inviting a teacher to help (Any two)
Why it would be helpful: e.g. better performance / more confidence / doubts cleared / teacher assistance (Any two)
Expression: Opening and closing sentences, syntax, vocabulary and punctuation.
key_points: Invitation (any one): e.g. please come / I invite you / we would like you to join
Details of the study group / how you plan to revise (any two): e.g. topic-wise discussion / shared notes / using online devices / discussion / inviting a teacher to help
Why it would be helpful (any two): e.g. better performance / more confidence / doubts cleared / teacher assistance
Expression: Opening and closing sentences, syntax, vocabulary and punctuation.
common_errors: Did not actually invite the classmate
Did not separate revision plan from benefits
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Content: some mentioned the plan but forgot to invite the classmate, or asked the classmate to form the group. The revision plan and its benefits were often not distinguished; 'revise' was used as a point instead of naming the revision activities. Format: 'February' misspelt or abbreviated, year omitted, date in numerals; impersonal salutations ('Dear Friend', 'Dear Classmate'); subscription errors ('Your friend, ABC', full name, 'Yours lovingly friend', 'Your's'); cursive 'y'. Expression was comparatively better than in Question 1, though spelling errors were frequent.

format_elements: Date (day, month written in full, year)
Salutation addressing the recipient by name or relation (e.g. Dear Riya / Dear Grandma)
Body: opening sentence, content paragraphs, closing sentence
Subscription (e.g. Yours lovingly / Yours affectionately), no apostrophe in 'Yours'

examples: we would like you to join

content_requirements.element: Details of the study group / how you plan to revise

writing_task.expression_criteria: Opening and closing sentences, syntax, vocabulary and punctuation.

marking_schemes.question_text: The drainage system in your locality needs repair. Write a letter to the Municipal Commissioner stating the problems caused due to this. Suggest solutions to improve the situation.
marking_schemes.scheme_text:
Format (Formal letter)
Content
Complaints: e.g. flooded streets / overflowing gutters (Any two)
Suggestions: e.g. replace the old drains / repair drains / desilting / unplug / clean / sanitization (Any two)
Expression: Opening and closing sentences, syntax, vocabulary and punctuation.
key_points: Complaints (any two): e.g. flooded streets / overflowing gutters
Suggestions (any two): e.g. replace the old drains / repair drains / desilting / unplug / clean / sanitization
Expression: Opening and closing sentences, syntax, vocabulary and punctuation.
common_errors: Restated the question instead of naming problems
Vague request ('look into the matter') instead of specific solutions
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Content: some merely reproduced the information in the question without identifying further problems; others raised poor hygiene, foul odour, waterlogged roads, pests and disease. Many failed to propose specific solutions and only asked the Commissioner to 'look into the matter'. Format: February errors, missing year, numeric date; 'Respected Sir'; 'Yours sincerely'/'Your humble servant', 'XYZ' or first name only; 'Your's'. Expression was better than previous years; most kept a formal tone.

format_elements: Date (day, month written in full, year)
Receiver's address beginning with the designation, then organisation and city
Salutation (Sir / Madam / Dear Sir / Dear Madam), not 'Respected Sir'
Body: opening sentence, content paragraphs, closing sentence
writing_task.expression_criteria: Opening and closing sentences, syntax, vocabulary and punctuation.

marking_schemes.question_text: Your school is organising an Inter House Non-Flame Cooking Competition. Write a notice informing the students about the event.
marking_schemes.scheme_text:
Creative Title: Master Chef / Little Chef / Tickle your Tastebuds / Snack Time
Event: Annual Inter House Non-Flame Cooking Competition
Date: Accept single date, for example a week or fortnight away from the date of writing
Time: 10.00 a.m. - 3.00 p.m. [Accept capital letters for a.m., p.m.]
Venue: smaller place to larger
Participation: All pupils who wish to register should give their names to the Vice Principal/etc. on or before/by ...
[Recommended: no word from the question is used for the creative title]
key_points: Creative Title: Master Chef / Little Chef / Tickle your Tastebuds / Snack Time
Event: Annual Inter House Non-Flame Cooking Competition
Date: Accept single date, for example a week or fortnight away from the date of writing
Time: 10.00 a.m. - 3.00 p.m. [Accept capital letters for a.m., p.m.]
Participation: All pupils who wish to register should give their names to the Vice Principal/etc. on or before/by ...
[Recommended: no word from the question is used for the creative title]
common_errors: Registration details missing or deadline after the event
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Many struggled to frame a relevant creative title; vague titles ('Compete to Win', 'Art Attack') or words from the question ('cooking') were used. 'Inter-House' was often omitted. Event dates were too early, too close to or too far from the exam date, or carried wrong months/years. Venues were not given smaller-to-larger; registration details were omitted or the deadline fell after/too close to the event. Format and paragraph sequencing were often not followed.

examples: Annual Inter House Non-Flame Cooking Competition
Accept single date, for example a week or fortnight away from the date of writing
10.00 a.m. - 3.00 p.m. [Accept capital letters for a.m., p.m.]
All pupils who wish to register should give their names to the Vice Principal/etc. on or before/by ...

penalised: Words from the question used in the creative title (recommended against)

Your school is organising an Inter House Non-Flame Cooking Competition.
Write an email to a famous chef, inviting him/her to judge the event.
marking_schemes.scheme_text:
E-mail id (recipient; official, with @ and provider)
Subject
Salutation
Opening sentence
Closing sentence
Subscription
Expression - All details of the notice are to be included in the e-mail.
key_points: E-mail id (recipient; official, with @ and provider)
Expression - All details of the notice are to be included in the e-mail.

marking_schemes.examiner_notes: A few confused 'chef' with 'chief'. Inappropriate email ids ('famouschef...', 'principal@gmail.com') were used. The subject line was mostly correct, but some omitted it or wrote the date. Informal salutations ('Hi Gordon'); subscription errors as in letters. Some omitted the date, time and venue from the notice; some used flowery language and irrelevant details.

format_elements: E-mail id (recipient; official, with @ and provider)
writing_task.expression_criteria: Expression - All details of the notice are to be included in the e-mail.

For each word given below choose the correct meaning (as used in the passage) from the options provided:
1. dilapidated (line 6)
options: (a) faded and yellow
(b) new and shining
(c) tightly wrapped
(d) old and ragged
marking_schemes.scheme_text: (d) old and ragged

stimulus.text:
"This is your teacher today. He's going to show you all sorts of things." With that the headmaster introduced a new teacher. Totto-chan took a good look at him but he wasn't dressed like a teacher at all. He wore a striped cotton jacket and he had a towel hanging around his neck. His trousers were of dyed cotton and were full of patches. Instead of shoes, he wore thick socks, while on his head was a rather dilapidated straw hat.

The children were all assembled by the pond at the temple.

As she stared at the teacher, Totto-chan thought that she had seen him before. "Where?" she wondered. His kindly face was sunburnt and full of wrinkles. She suddenly remembered!

"Aren't you the farmer who works in the field by the stream?" she asked him, delighted.

"That's right," said the 'teacher', with a smile wrinkling up his face. "You pass my place every time you go to the village! That's my field. That one over there full of mustard blossoms."

"Wow! So you're going to be our teacher today," cried the children excitedly.

"No!" said the man, waving his hand in front of his face. "I'm not a teacher! I'm just a farmer. Your headmaster just asked me to do it, that's all."

"Oh yes, he is, he's your farming teacher," said the headmaster, standing beside him. "He very kindly agreed to teach you how to plant a field."

At an elementary school, anyone who taught the children anything would probably have to have teaching qualifications, but the headmaster didn't worry about things like that. He thought it important for children to learn by actually seeing things done.

"Let's begin then," said the farming teacher.

The farming teacher told the children to get spades and other tools from the car and started them on weeding. He told them all about weeds: how hardy they were; how some grew faster than crops and hid the sun from them; how weeds were good hiding places for bad insects; and how weeds could be a nuisance by taking all the nourishment from the soil. He taught them one thing after another. And while he talked, his hands never stopped pulling out weeds.

The children did the same. Then the teacher showed them how to dig, how to make furrows; how to spread fertilizer; and everything else you had to do to grow things in a field, explaining as he demonstrated.

A little snake put its head out and very nearly bit the hand of Ta-chan, one of the older boys, but the farming teacher reassured him, "The snakes here are not poisonous, and they won't hurt you if you don't hurt them."

Besides teaching the children how to plant a field, the farming teacher told them interesting things about insects, birds, and butterflies, about the weather, and about all sorts of other things.
stimulus.source: Adapted from 'Totto-chan - The Little Girl at the Window' by Tetsuko Kuroyanagi
stimulus.line_references: Line numbers in questions refer to the printed paper's margin numbering.

marking_schemes.question_text:
For each word given below choose the correct meaning (as used in the passage) from the options provided:
2. elementary (line 21)
options: (a) primary
(b) special
(c) secondary
(d) village
marking_schemes.scheme_text: (a) primary
marking_schemes.model_answer: (a) primary
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: 'Elementary' was incorrectly identified as (c) 'secondary' by many and (d) 'village' by a few.

The headmaster said he was their farming teacher who had agreed to teach them how to plant a field
marking_schemes.model_answer: The farmer claimed he was an ordinary farmer but the headmaster said he was a farming teacher; he had agreed to teach them how to plant a field.
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: An analytical question requiring interpretation. Many answered correctly; some were confused or superficial, and several copied portions of the text without analysis.

stimulus.text:
"This is your teacher today. He's going to show you all sorts of things." With that the headmaster introduced a new teacher. Totto-chan took a good look at him but he wasn't dressed like a teacher at all. He wore a striped cotton jacket and he had a towel hanging around his neck. His trousers were of dyed cotton and were full of patches. Instead of shoes, he wore thick socks, while on his head was a rather dilapidated straw hat.

The children were all assembled by the pond at the temple.

As she stared at the teacher, Totto-chan thought that she had seen him before. "Where?" she wondered. His kindly face was sunburnt and full of wrinkles. She suddenly remembered!

"Aren't you the farmer who works in the field by the stream?" she asked him, delighted.

"That's right," said the 'teacher', with a smile wrinkling up his face. "You pass my place every time you go to the village! That's my field. That one over there full of mustard blossoms."

"Wow! So you're going to be our teacher today," cried the children excitedly.

"No!" said the man, waving his hand in front of his face. "I'm not a teacher! I'm just a farmer. Your headmaster just asked me to do it, that's all."

"Oh yes, he is, he's your farming teacher," said the headmaster, standing beside him. "He very kindly agreed to teach you how to plant a field."

At an elementary school, anyone who taught the children anything would probably have to have teaching qualifications, but the headmaster didn't worry about things like that. He thought it important for children to learn by actually seeing things done.

"Let's begin then," said the farming teacher.

The farming teacher told the children to get spades and other tools from the car and started them on weeding. He told them all about weeds: how hardy they were; how some grew faster than crops and hid the sun from them; how weeds were good hiding places for bad insects; and how weeds could be a nuisance by taking all the nourishment from the soil. He taught them one thing after another. And while he talked, his hands never stopped pulling out weeds.

The children did the same. Then the teacher showed them how to dig, how to make furrows; how to spread fertilizer; and everything else you had to do to grow things in a field, explaining as he demonstrated.

A little snake put its head out and very nearly bit the hand of Ta-chan, one of the older boys, but the farming teacher reassured him, "The snakes here are not poisonous, and they won't hurt you if you don't hurt them."

Besides teaching the children how to plant a field, the farming teacher told them interesting things about insects, birds, and butterflies, about the weather, and about all sorts of other things.
stimulus.source: Adapted from 'Totto-chan - The Little Girl at the Window' by Tetsuko Kuroyanagi
stimulus.line_references: Line numbers in questions refer to the printed paper's margin numbering.

marking_schemes.question_text: (d) Why was the headmaster right in inviting the new teacher to take a class?
marking_schemes.scheme_text: A wide variety of plausible answers.
key_points: Any plausible, text-supported reason, e.g. the headmaster believed children learn best by actually seeing things done; the farmer had practical knowledge and taught by demonstration
marking_schemes.model_answer: The headmaster believed it was important for children to learn by actually seeing things done, and the farmer, with his practical knowledge, could demonstrate how to plant a field.
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: A higher-order thinking question. Most answered correctly; some merely copied text without analysis.

marking_schemes.question_text: In not more than 50 words, give an account of what the farmer taught the children that day.
marking_schemes.scheme_text:
Points:
1. told them about weeds / hardy / some grow faster
2. hid the sun
3. good hiding places for insects
4. nuisance / taking nourishment from soil
5. how to dig
6. make furrows
7. spread fertilizer
8. everything else you had to grow in a field / how to plant a field / demonstrated
9. snakes... / insects, birds and butterflies (accept both as separate points)
10. weather
(Any 6 points in correct sequence)
key_points: told them about weeds / hardy / some grow faster
everything else you had to grow in a field / how to plant a field / demonstrated
snakes... / insects, birds and butterflies (accept both as separate points)
common_errors: Started from the wrong section of the passage
Points in rough draft missing from fair draft
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Most wrote the summary well and identified most key points. Some focused only on weeds; a few exceeded the word limit; several wrote barely 20 words and omitted points. Others began from the wrong section and missed points; some dropped points from rough to fair draft or left the fair draft incomplete.

marking_schemes.question_text:
Fill in each of the numbered blanks with the correct form of the word given in brackets. Do not copy the passage but write in correct serial order the word or phrase appropriate to the blank space.
Example: The road northwards through Tanganyika was narrow and often deeply rutted. And once I (0) ______ (see) a very large brown cobra. Answer: saw
It (1) ______ (glide) slowly over the ruts in the road ahead of me. It was seven or eight feet long and (2) ______ (hold) its flat spoon-shaped head six inches up in the air. I (3) ______ (stop) the car smartly so as not (4) ______ (run) over it. To be truthful, I was so (5) ______ (frighten), I (6) ______ (go) quickly into reverse and (7) ______ (keep) backing away. The fearsome thing (8) ______ (disappear) into the undergrowth.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: [0. saw] (1) glided / was gliding  (2) held  (3) stopped  (4) to run  (5) frightened  (6) went  (7) kept  (8) disappeared / had disappeared
marking_schemes.model_answer:
(1) glided
(2) held
(3) stopped
(4) to run
(5) frightened
(6) went
(7) kept
(8) disappeared
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Many struggled with tense: 'glide'/'gliding' (1), 'holded' (2), 'stopd' (3), 'runned' (4), 'frightening'/'frighten' (5), 'goes'/'gone' (6), 'keep'/'keeped' (7), 'dissappear(ed)' (8).

marking_schemes.question_text:
Fill in the blanks with appropriate words.
(a) He acted according ______ my instructions.
(b) They scaled up the wall ______ means of a rope.
(c) Gina has a passion ______ music.
(d) Father patted Jai ______ his back for his good results.
(e) I have not seen Sonia ______ last May.
(f) They worked ______ the night to complete the project on time.
(g) Ms. Sharma refused to buy a new car because the cost was ______ her means.
(h) Saif knew nothing about the event since it had happened ______ he was born.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: (a) to  (b) by  (c) for  (d) on  (e) since  (f) through / throughout / into  (g) beyond  (h) before
marking_schemes.model_answer:
(a) to
(b) by
(c) for
(d) on
(e) since
(f) through
(g) beyond
(h) before
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Most answered (a), (d), (e), (h) correctly. In (b) many wrote 'with'; some wrote 'in'/'of' in (c). In (f) 'from'/'along' and in (g) 'within'/'against'/'in' were common errors; (f) and (g) were hardest.

(b) All other kings are greater than Samudragupta.
(c) Very few Indian kings were as great as Samudragupta.
(d) Some Indian kings are greatest as Samudragupta.

marking_schemes.question_text:
Choose the correct option and rewrite the sentence according to the instruction given after each.
2. One should keep one's promises.
(Begin with: Promises ...)
options: (a) Promises should keep one.
(b) One's promises are not meant to be kept.
(c) Promises should be kept.
(d) Promises are one's to keep.
marking_schemes.scheme_text: (c) Promises should be kept.
marking_schemes.model_answer: (c) Promises should be kept.
marking_schemes.examiner_notes: Some chose (b) or (d), possibly from careless reading; active-to-passive conversion caused errors.

marking_schemes.question_text:
Choose the correct option and rewrite the sentence according to the instruction given after each.
3. He said, "I have passed the examination."
(Begin: He said that.........)
options: (a) He said that he had passed the examination.
(b) He said that he passed the examination.
(c) He said that he has passed the examination.
(d) He said that he will pass the examination.
marking_schemes.correct_answer: (a) He said that he had passed the examination.

marking_schemes.question_text:

1: Teach story-planning techniques and the elements and structure of an original short story
Guide students to place given words or sentences exactly where instructed
Teach use of sensory details (sight, sound, smell, taste, touch) in descriptions
Teach argument construction with a clear stand, two or three main points and illustrations
Encourage broad interpretation of the picture beyond listing its contents
2: Teach correct formal and friendly letter formats; refer to specimen letters on the CISCE website
Read the topic carefully and address the premise, problems and plausible solutions
Write the full date with the month spelt out correctly; receiver's address begins with designation
3: Use model emails to teach format, structure and language
Use the event name in the subject line
Keep notice and email details (date, time, venue) consistent
4: Practise contextual vocabulary, synonyms and antonyms
Teach exact quotation when a sentence is asked for
Develop inferential and higher-order thinking skills
Practise summary writing with grids, rough and fair drafts
5: Reinforce tense rules and regular/irregular verb forms
Practise transformations: voice, reported speech, unless/if...not, too...to/so...that, degrees of comparison, not only...but also

difficult_topics: Punctuation in direct speech; commas, full stops, question marks
Addressing all parts of letter questions
confusions: Q1(i): given opening words not used as the start of a structured plot; story turned into a narrative
Q1(v): no clear connection between essay and picture
Q3: both notice and email had to be written; some wrote only one
